Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

Following last year’s near 4% downturn in metal demand, we have noticed a continued pick-up in refined copper offtake, whether it has initially been due to the need to re-stock, or subsequently in end-user demand itself.  The 8.6% improvement anticipated this year already takes us beyond the former global record demand level of 17.955Mt set in 2008, and if it were not for some of the more systemic lingering issues (such as tighter credit availability), the copper market probably would have forgotten all about the “global economic crisis” already.  Looking at the bald numbers alone, then, one could say that in terms of copper demand, we have made a “recovery” – and somewhat sooner than everyone was expecting.  Expected growth for the next two years of between 5-6% should tap into the improving construction markets globally which, arguably, will be the last important sector to “recover”. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1.2% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~18.8Mt in 2013 to ~13.3Mt in 2025.  However, note that this rate of decline excludes our mine disruption allowance (5% of initial mine production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.5Mt/a in 2011, ~0.7Mt/a in 2013, 6.1Mt/a in 2020 and ~13.8Mt/a by 2025. 

Once again we have lowered our global smelter production capability estimates for this year, but, unlike in our last report, we have consistently lowered our smelter estimates through to 2014.  The lower estimates for this year reflect smelter cuts because of sustained concentrate shortages.  Further out, the increased smelter production capability forecasts primarily reflect the potential for increased production from Chile’s Altonorte and Caletones smelters, Mexico’s La Caridad smelter and China’s Kangxi smelter.  We now expect base case global copper smelter production capability to increase by 5.4% this year, to 14.9Mt, relative to production in 2009, and by 10% and 8.9% in 2011 and 2012 to 16.4Mt and 17.9Mt respectively. 

Primary copper supply growth during H1 has been restricted due to low availability of concentrate feed, and smelters/refiners have had to turn to secondary materials to bridge the gap.  We expect global refined copper production to increase by just 2.3% this year to ~18.764Mt.  2011’s refined production growth of 3.6%, and even the following year’s 7.4%, will be insufficient to outweigh our anticipated demand growth over the period, however, leaving us with a deficit of

almost 450kt in 2011 and a balanced market for 2012.  By 2013, though, we are expecting considerable supply-side increases to outweigh average demand growth forecasts quite considerably, leaving an extended period to 2019 of structural market excess to the tune of an _average_ of 400kt/a metal (although when measuring projected inventories in days, only three of these seven years could be described as particularly excessive). 

From a fundamental perspective we expect prices to remain on their upward trend into 2011 to average $7791/t ($3.53/lb) in constant 2010$.  The hefty increase in refined production in 2012 should provide some relief to the market, and we would expect copper quotes to reflect that; our average price forecast for that year now stands at $7445/t ($3.38/lb) in constant 2010$, but with the market finely balanced in that year (we show a “surplus” of just 11kt), it would not take much of a supply-side disruption to raise the upward risk profile on prices again. 

Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, will trend lower from 76 days at the end of last year, to 55 days in 2012, but are projected to rise steadily, increasing from 58 days in 2013 to a cyclical peak of 91 days in 2019.  Reflecting this, average prices are expected to fall to the cyclical low of $3748/t ($1.70c/lb) in constant 2010$ by 2019 (or $4934/t, $2.24c/lb in current dollars).

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Refined copper consumption much stronger than expected** A combination of heavier re-stocking of downstream products during the first quarter this year in most leading consumer regions of the world, plus stronger underlying demand especially in China for the first half, has resulted in a significant increase in global primary copper consumption since our last quarterly report.  Equally, upward revisions to demand data for 2009 in the USA offset minor losses elsewhere to leave last year’s demand down by a smaller -3.6% (vs. -3.8%) on 2008 at 17.3Mt.  This year’s recovery is now looking to be healthier than our prior forecast of 6.1% at 8.6%, taking global demand up to 18.8Mt, with most regions sharing in the widespread improvement.  This is far beyond the pre-crisis 2008 demand level of just below 18Mt, and reflects the general disparity between apparent metals demand and the day-to-day sentiment of economic malaise. 

**Stronger 2010 recovery puts 2011 year-on-year growth lower** Having increased our forecast demand growth for 2010, the year-on-year percentage growth for next year is lower at 5.8% vs. the 6.8% we were predicting in our second quarter report.  However, in volume terms 2011 is 335kt higher at almost 19.9Mt.  While Chinese demand growth is leading the way, it is by no means the only geographic region of strength in the near term.  We expect European demand to increase by 5.3% this year and a further 1.4% in 2011, and North America

n demand to rise by 4.3% in 2010 and by 2% next year.  Over the long term, however, it is Chinese copper use and Asian demand in general which will sustain the metal going forward.  China’s continued investment and need to modernise should keep copper demand at a long-term rate of 6% p.a., while Asian and Latin American developing economies will also chip in with demand growth rates of between 4.5-5% p.a.  Thus global refined copper consumption will rise from 17.3Mt at the end of 2009 to 30.3Mt by the end of our forecast period.

## China 

**Leading indicators supportive of slowdown policy** Economic data for China over the summer months continued to support our view that the country is adequately managing its soft landing for the second half of this year.  Fixed asset investment increased by 24.8% YoY in the first 8 months, which was 0.1 percentage point lower from that for the first seven months.  Investment in property development rose 34.1% year-on-year in August, compared with 33% for July and 36.7% for the first eight months. The Central government has begun to consider a fiscal stimulus exit based on the macro-economical conditions during the January to September period. 

**The growth of China's industrial value-added output accelerated to 13.9% year-on-year in August from July's 13.4%** The growth rate for the first eight months was 16.6%, down 0.4% from the January to July period.  The strength in heavy industrial production and fixed investment may in part be due to a re-stocking after the de-stocking in early summer and after the government emphasised the importance of maintaining growth at the end of July.  However, some local governments became increasingly worried about achieving their energy efficiency targets and started to cut power to energy-intensive sectors at the end of August.  If investment, and hence demand, for heavy industrial products, continues to hold up stronger than expected for the rest of the year, then achieving the energy efficiency target will have to rely more on supply restraint – power cuts and capacity closures. 

**Domestic demand was stronger than expected** China's retail sales of consumer goods in August increased by 18.4% year-on-year; urban consumption was up 18.8%

and rural consumption increased by 15.9%.  Housing sales volume started to recover in August, and this trend might continue to the end of this year. 

**August exports continued to weaken** While year-ago growth was a strong 34.4%, the August change fell a large 2.7%, and it was the third consecutive decline.  Imports increased by 2.5% m/m, after falling for two consecutive months.

The year-ago change was also a higher 35.2%.  The stronger result is consistent with growing signs of stabilisation in the heavy industrial sector, while also suggesting that exports are softening, but not collapsing.  Compared with the high base of Q4 2009, China’s economic growth will continue to slow.  Q4 GDP growth should be in the region of 8.0-8.5% year-on-year due to the impact of the property tightening, energy saving measures, and the expected soft exports. 

**Energy saving measures should have little impact on copper demand** Some major copper fabricators in Zhejiang province mentioned that electricity supply has been better in September than it was in August due to lower electricity demand from air conditioning use.  Recent power brownouts and government-driven electricity cutbacks to high powerconsuming sectors in Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces will limit forward-looking semis output from these regions.  With Zhejiang accounting for 30% of the nation’s copper consumption, this should firstly draw down product inventories as consumers scramble to cover for the anticipated Q4 demand.  If the brownouts continue into October – or even until the end of the year, as some sources say - then copper semis manufacturing will pick up at idle capacity elsewhere. Therefore, we do not believe that this government-led initiative to improve energy efficiency by 20% by the end of the year will stifle copper processing, but merely re-locate it. 

**Mixed real estate measures** Floor space for new-build housing increased by 66.1% year-on-year in the first eight months, reflecting more new housing projects under construction.  However, figures for floor space of completed housing increased by less than 11% to July, and it actually fell by 2.1% in August, reflecting that some investors have postponed completing the projects due to current weak demand, and this will have a knock-on effect for building wire and associated construction products. 

**Lower ACR tube output in August** ACR tube production continued to slow down in August due to the falling demand for air conditioning and lower exports.  Imposing preliminary dumping rates on imported refined copper tube from China in USA began to take their toll on Chinese exports of ACR tube since May.  Although refined copper tube exports in July increased by 8% year-on-year, export growth between January and July has been flat.  We expect ACR tube exports will continue to fall in the coming months because of the disruption to s

uppliers. Usually, air conditioner makers need three months to test new ACR tube in their production lines, and after this time we would expect that US-based air conditioner makers will change their Chinese ACR tube suppliers. **Wire rod markets flat in early September** There are no signs that wire rod production in September has improved over August, and this is contrary to the expectations of most wire rod makers. De-stocking by auto makers and the slowdown in the export markets of some electrical home appliances represent some of the reasons at least for this aberration. **Power industry investment up marginally** According to the latest data issued by China Electricity Council, the investment in power industry in the first eight months reached 365.9Bn RMB ($54.4Bn), increasing by 1.7% year-onyear. Investments in power generation increased by 15.5% year-on-year, reaching 196.6Bn RMB ($29.2Bn) and it accounted for 53.7% of total power industry investment. Investment in the power grid fell by 11.1% year-on-year, and this explains the ongoing weakness in the demand for power cable. ###### **Chinese production of copper and copper alloy products - (kt)** 50 % change Production 3000

**Healthy growth in Chinese copper demand during the forecast period** This year, despite all the debate and concern regarding the enforced slowdown in the Chinese economy, we remain confident that copper demand will increase by 13% year-on-year to 7.3Mt. Equally, although the country’s primary copper-refining sector has drawn down on large supplies of scrap there has not been a comparable appetite for scrap from the semis sector. Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 6% p.a., rising from ~6.5Mt at the end of 2009 to ~16.5Mt by 2025. As of this month, the USA is officially out of recession, but the run-up to the important November elections will continue to focus on the poor employment figures and the heavily flawed “debate” over personal taxation rates. Meanwhile, for much of this year, metals demand has far outpaced most expectations, with manufacturing activity having been much stronger than expected. **Manufacturing coming into line with demand** However, the main debate for metals demand this year has been the re-stocking cycle and if/when underlying demand would take over. What we have seen in copper and other metals is that producers and consumers at all links along the chain have been as cautious in re-stocking as they have been in matching new fabrication rates to orders. In the US, at least, we believe that the re-stocking phase is coming to an end, and that new manufacturing rates are now matching demand much more closely. Effectively, this means a continuation of the “hand-to-mouth” existence, with all elements in the supply-demand chain keeping stock to a minimum, even at the risk of not being able to satisfy spot market requirements as they arise. This is not so encouraging for near-term metals demand because other macro-economic indicators, such as retail sales and employment figures, are weak, and this is likely to cap consumption. **Improvement in wire rod demand** Reflecting the improvement in manufacturing activity, US demand for copper wire rod, according to the American Bureau of Metals Statistics, increased during the second quarter for the first time since Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2010 Page 7 of 41 Copper Long-term Outlook Q4 2007 – although we should bear in mind that Q2 2009 was the worst quarterly period in history. H1 rod demand was up by 4.6% on the same period last year. June domestic shipments were 18.4% higher than a year ago at 110.7kt, the highest since March. Furthermore, rod inventories were down by 25% at the end of June vs. end-April’s 27.6kt at 20.4kt, and even though this could have been partly due to so

me summer shutdowns, it leaves the potential open for a sharp improvement in Q3 demand. 

**Construction sector still struggling** With the construction accounting for 50% of US copper demand, it is difficult to remain optimistic when most indices for the sector continue to fall.  Despite the lowest mortgage rates in years and relatively low buying prices, sales of existing homes in the US (which account for 90% of total home sales) fell in July by over 27% to a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 3.83M units.  This was the lowest rate in 15 years, according to the National Association of Realtors, and the largest month-on-month fall since 1968.  Furthermore, the decline was noted across all geographic regions but particularly apparent in the low- to mid-price range which had benefitted the most from the now-expired government tax breaks up to April this year.  Meanwhile, sales of new homes (the “top-up” 10% of total sales) fell by 12.4% in July from June to an annualised rate of 226k units, and this was the slowest rate since records began in 1963. 

The inventory of unsold homes now extends over 12 months at current sales rates, which is the highest in ten years and more than double the level that is usually accepted as being sufficient to support prices and ongoing sales.  Tightening lending standards have offset the potential improvement in home sales that would normally be seen with mortgage interest rates that are frequently under 5%. The threat of unemployment is also hindering mortgage applications. Meanwhile, the home builder index fell again by a point in August to 13, which indicates that any improvement in the construction sector for the next six months is remote. 

**Auto sales strong in July but flop in August…** Other sectors that are important to copper demand in the US, though, remain strong.  Total vehicle assemblies, on a seasonally-adjusted basis, rose to an annualised rate of 8.53M units, which is the highest rate in two years.  The gains came almost entirely from the light trucks market, with car production relatively unchanged. Inventories decreased by three days to 52 days, indicating that producers continue to show restraint.  Automotive sales were also strong in July, up by 5.2% year on year to 1.05M units ( _vs._ 984k units in June), but fleet sales rose by a much stronger rate (up 40% year on year) than retail (down by 3.8% year on year), and this is masking the underlying weakness in consumer demand.  Having said this, early data for August point to a sharp decline in auto sales, with model-year close-out promotions failing to catch public attention, and the hope is that Labor Day sales on the first Monday into September were better. 

**Brass mills report positive order levels during Q2** Following the path of its sister products in wire rod, US brass mill products output trended lower over the months of April-May, as reflected in the most recent data.  Copper and copper alloy semis output of 409kt (metric) for Januar

y to May this year was up by 13% on the same period last year, although that did cover the trough in the cycle. Although pure copper semis production tailed off slightly (from 203kt to 194kt), output of _alloy_ semis surged from 163kt to 222kt. However, as with wire rod data, we note that the recent high was in March; with the house buying incentives falling away in April-May, we doubt that these markets will pick up before this year is out. According to our sources, the earlier positive demand reflected a combination of re-stocking and the possible introduction of an anti-dumping duty on copper tube imports from both Mexico and China. Copper tube manufacturers reported to us that the rising interest in copper tube reflected the joint investigation by the Commerce Department and International Trade Commission (ITC) into whether imports of Mexican and Chinese copper tube were being sold below market value in the US. In the middle of August the Commerce Department and the ITC introduced a preliminary dumping margin of 30.9% on all Mexican tube imports (with 29.52% on those from producer IUSA and 32.27% on those from Nacobre, specifically) and a margin of between 10.26% and 60.5% on all Chinese tube imports. The contraction reflects structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies. Imports, rather than domestic production, will satisfy domestic copper demand. Therefore, while the region’s wire and cable markets will be supported by the upgrading of much of its other infrastructure, this will not Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2010 Page 8 of 41 Copper Long-term Outlook necessarily result in increased production of North American copper wire rod. By 2025 we forecast that North American consumption will total ~1.23Mt. This will account for 4% of the global total compared with 10% in 2009. ## Europe **European copper demand increased to 3.6Mt** We have

increased our forecast for European copper demand this year from 3.51Mt to 3.61Mt since our second quarter report, given the stronger first four to five months of the year than previously anticipated, especially in the industrial powerhouses of Germany and Italy. That said, weakening economic data into July and August suggest that the second half will result in slightly lower copper demand. The acceleration in growth rates seen earlier in Q2 and before has been largely reliant upon government policy and the inventory re-stocking cycle, and moving forward we are probably heading for a higher weighting of austerity measures which will restrain growth well into 2011. Early August indicators show lower performances than in July, but this might still be a reflection of summer shut-downs rather than the start of the more widespread downturn in business levels. **Germany leads the europack** The EU manufacturing PMI’s rebounded in July, with Germany leading the way. Here, auto production in particular has continued to recover, despite July’s seasonal drop in auto output of 418kt units (down by 2.9% year on year). While there is widespread expectation that the second half of this year will see some level of decline from Q2 levels, for the present time we are not seeing any dramatic reversal of these gains. Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has benefitted from the stronger auto and energy sectors, and posted its fifth straight quarterly improvement in aggregate wire rod and shapes production. At 260kt for the March-June quarter (Q3 for Aurubis’ reporting), this exceeded the 246kt produced in the final quarter ahead of the economic crisis (calendar Q3 2008). In other products, Aurubis has continued to increase output of pre-rolled strip (56kt in Q2 vs. 50kt in Q1 2010 – matching Q2 2008’s 58kt level), while strip and wire from the former Prymetall subsidiary held steady at 13.1kt. **KME looking to positive second half** KME, which claims to be the world’s largest semis fabricator, selling 437kt of copper and alloy semis in 2009 from manufacturing plants in Germany, Italy, France, UK, Spain and China, reported a 21% (+46kt, to 264kt) increase in its output of copper and copper alloy products in H1 from a year earlier. Robust orders from the auto and electronics sectors and domestic appliance manufacturing helped to offset weak demand from the construction sector, which accounts for 40% of KME’s sales by application. Even so, compared to 2006 total sales of 673kt, it is clear that the impact on KME’s business of the downturn in construction is significant, and so we expect to wait for another year or more before we see business activity levels approach those heights again. ###### **Eurozone economic recovery wavering** 65

**Romania’s wire rod sector draws on imports** Earlier this year we noted that Romania’s sole copper wire rod facility was rumoured to have been closed down during the final quarter of 2009, presumably a victim of the global recession. Given the fact that both domestic production and imports of cathode have been zero this year, we suspected that the Cuprom wire rod plant at Zalau had gone the same way as its sister smelter-refinery complex at Baie Mare and closed. The company has since confirmed to us that the rod plant did in fact close in September 2009, having produced just 10kt of wire rod from cathode stock alone. Instead, Cuprom has turned to imports of rod to keep its wire-making equipment gainfully employed. Rod imports in 2009 of 28.6kt picked up a notch starting from the final quarter of the year to average 3.3kt/m, and this average rate has increased yet further to 3.7kt/m from January-May this year. Cuprom’s Zalau rod plant produced an average of 25kt/a between 2005 and 2008, but this slipped to 10kt last year, with domestic material being increasingly replaced by imports. Now it appears that Romania’s entire 30-40kt/a rod market of recent years is being supplied by imported stock, with rod makers in Italy, Germany, Greece and Belgium proving to be the main Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2010 Page 9 of 41 Copper Long-term Outlook beneficiaries. Consequently, we have reduced our Romanian primary copper consumption forecast for this year from 12kt to 4kt. **Polish wire rod production increased** First half refined cathode production figures from KGHM, plus trade data to May, have prompted us to increase Poland’s rod production forecast for this year. Higher cathode production and net imports should enable KGHM to produce c.205kt of wire rods this year at its Cedynia facility, _vs._ our former forecast of 156kt and 2009’s actual output of 191kt. Judging by the company’s H1 cathode performance, though, H2 rod output will tail off slightly as 268kt (52%) of the full year’s cathode target of 512kt has already been produced. Clearly rod sales are proving to be more resilient than we had anticipated, largely due to the improving construction sector, and this has encouraged us to raise forecast 2011 rod output as well, from our former 165kt to 212kt. This keeps in-house conversion of cathode to wire rod at c.40%, which is in line with recent years, albeit slightly lower than the 48% seen earlier this decade. KGHM is continuing to improve the capacity utilisation rate from its value-added product range via the UPCAST oxygen-free rod line investment, which it completed in September 2007. Last year, 13.8kt came off this 15kt/a capacity line, up from 11.8kt the prior year. ###### **European refined copper consumption – kt** ||||||||**20**

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2010 Page 14 of 41 Copper Long-term Outlook # Supply analysis ## Changes to mine production forecasts since Q2 **Only small changes to our near-term mine outlook** Changes to our base case global mine production and _production capability_ estimates since our last quarterly report are detailed in the main report. The downgrades to our 2010 and 2011 figures of c.80kt and c.50kt, respectively, reflect disruptions and the deferral of mine re-starts. However, from 2012 onwards, we have considerably raised both our mine production and production capability estimates since our last report, reflecting upgrades to various mine projects into our base case. **Project deferrals result in lower mine production in the near term** Earlier this year we expressed concern as to whether copper mine disruptions moving forward would be as significant as they had been over the past five years. Some of this concern arose from the fact that a number of prominent mines actually exceeded their 2009 production guidance last year, thereby partially offsetting disruptions elsewhere. We questioned the need to apply a 6% generic initial disruption to our forecasts if, for example, the bottlenecks at manufacturers of equipment, spare parts and consumables were perhaps easing on the premise that these suppliers would surely increase their capacity to overcome these issues. We also wondered whether mining companies were applying more realistic, rather than optimistic production forecasts on the basis of prior experience. However, our latest assessment of the disruptions to date in 2010 tells us that a significant disruption allowance remains justified in the forecasts. Thus far this year we have identified over 500kt of losses from the concentrate producing sector and SxEw producers against an initial expectation of 840kt for 2010 as a whole. The major contributors to the disruptions to date include strikes at Vale’s Sudbury nickel/copper operations (now settled – see below) and at Voisey’s Bay (still ongoing), deferrals of high-grade ore extraction at Grasberg, a freeze on expenditure at First Quantum’s Frontier mine pending an ownership dispute, the slow reactivation of Cananea, earthquakes and lack of acid at some operations in Chile and the slow ramp up at Las Cruces in Spain. Typically, up to 75% of all disruptions are due to a

combination of technical issues, strikes and the slow ramp up of projects.  Assuming that high prices remain a feature of the market in the medium term then strikes will continue to be an issue, particularly in the Americas, although various companies have been successful in extending the life of labour contracts in order to prevent the frequency of industrial action.  Technical issues will remain a feature of the market although one might imagine that replacement lead times should be less than has been the case previously (for the reasons mentioned above).  The issue that we feel is most likely to dominate the disruption landscape over the next few years is the slow ramp up of projects, given the significant surge in capacity additions in the medium term.  To quantify this, over the period 2011 to 2013 gross additions to mine supply from greenfield and brownfield expansions are forecast to average 1.6Mt/a compared with an average of 0.75Mt/a over the period 2004 to 2009.

# Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type

of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

During 2009 copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) was 6.9Mt, representing 32% of total copper consumed.  Of all scrap consumed 59% went into direct use with smelting and refining absorbing 22% and 19% respectively.

Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to ex

plain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in

the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. # Economic analysis 

## Industrial Production Outlook 

The global economy is in a period of transition.  The strong recovery of the past year has weakened, as boosts to output from inventory adjustments and government stimulus have waned.  Although these boosts have been sufficient to ensure that growth for 2010 will be robust, 2011 will be a period of much more subdued growth. 

Recent economic performance has been distinctly mixed.  After recording strong gains through late 2009 and into early 2010, industrial activity in both Japan and the USA has lost momentum over recent months.  Contrastingly, in Europe we have seen some very robust growth through the second quarter, from Germany in particular.  So too have the Latin American economies posted solid improvements, and the major industrialising economies of Asia have been buoyant. However, there is a common thread that runs through all these economies.  Growth over the past year has been driven by temporary inventory adjustments and unsustainable stimulus measures, and deceleration is unavoidable.  Signs of this are already emerging.  Fixed asset investment growth slowed in China in August, retail spending in Brazil slowed in July, job creation in the USA has been weak, and in Germany we saw a contraction in machinery orders in July. 

Our base case forecast is for a double-dip recession to be avoided.  Nevertheless, significant structural problems pose a risk to growth – problems that have been masked by the recovery to date.  Excess capacity in some developed economies will weigh on investment, household debt in the USA is still a problem, concerns over sovereign debt pose a risk to financial markets, and stretched government finances are leading to hefty fiscal contraction for years to come.

Were such volumes to have been maintained for the rest of the year, Chinese vehicle production would have grown by another 46% this year. However, since March, vehicle production and sales have steadily declined, even though government incentives for cars were extended until the end of the year. The slowing can in part be attributed to increased uncertainty, stemming from the government crack-down on the high-end residential property market. Consequently, we expect Chinese vehicle production in 2010 to expand by just under 18% to 16.2 million units. Auto producers are adding very large amounts of capacity in China. The NDRC recently warned over a glut of excess capacity by 2015, when capacity reaches 31m vehicles per year, nearly twice the current domestic demand for vehicles. We expect Chinese production to grow at close to 7% per annum between now and 2015, implying that China will face overcapacity issues. However, given that we expect the number of vehicles on Chinese roads to grow by ~130% between now and 2020, as car ownership becomes affordable to a rapidly increasing proportion of the population, there is scope for demand to catch up with potential supply. ###### **Vehicle production by major Asian producers** 35

#### **Japan** After sliding lower through the second quarter, Japanese vehicle production has staged a come back in the past couple of months, resulting in production for 2010 to date being up 40% on the same period of last year. The gains of the past years have been due to improved demand for Japanese vehicles, both from overseas and in the domestic market, spurred on by green-car subsidies. However, Japanese producers are facing extremely challenging conditions over the short term. Japan’s own vehicle incentive scheme was brought to a close early, at the start of September, and it is likely we will see a period of lower sales in the coming months. In addition, overseas demand growth for Japanese

vehicles is expected to decline, with the strength of the Japanese yen making the country’s vehicles less competitive on the global market. We expect Japanese vehicle production to post growth of 15% for 2010, taking volumes to 9.1 million units – still 21% below the 2008 peak. While the market is expected to improve from late 2011, the weakness at the start of the year should result in 2011 production volumes being largely unchanged from this year. The long term prospects for Japanese auto production are not good. A declining population will reduce domestic demand, and Japanese auto makers will continue to relocate production facilities to lower cost locations, closer to end-use markets. Brazil’s robust economic growth is making first time vehicle purchases increasingly affordable to a larger proportion of the population. We expect vehicle production to expand by 11% this year, with growth between 5-10% per year out to 2015. Risks come primarily from Brazil’s road infrastructure, which is sorely lacking at present.
